 Pinned Updated   Nov. 3, 2026, 9:31 p.m. ET Reid J. Epstein and Kellen Browning 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Democrats notched a series of early victories and strong showings in states and districts where Republicans have won by large margins for years as the midterms offered voters the chance to deliver their first national mandate on President Trump’s second term.
 Democrats flipped the Senate seat in North Carolina and maintained control of seats in Georgia and New Hampshire, according to The Associated Press. And they flipped their first House seat of the night in western North Carolina.
 Races have yet to be called in South Carolina and Texas, where Democrats fielded strong and well-funded Senate candidates against Republicans considered their party’s weakest nominees. In each, the Democratic candidates are posting margins unthinkable for their party in counties that have reported the vast majorities of their votes.
 Republicans’ redistricting effort appears to have failed to yield the sweeping victories in House races that they intended. Democrats have already won three districts in Florida that Republicans redrew to be favorable for themselves, and the North Carolina seat Democrats flipped was also part of the Republican redistricting effort. 
 In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, became the first Black woman to be elected governor in the country’s history. She is the first Democrat elected to lead the state since 1998. 
 In Washington, Mr. Trump is watching the election results from the White House and posting criticism of the Fox News coverage on his social media site. He celebrated a Republican victory in Guam but has yet to speak at length about results in the 50 states.
 Democratic candidates have blamed Mr. Trump, and the war he started this year in Iran, for the economic hardships that have driven a current of frustration across the nation. Republicans have focused on portraying their Democratic opponents as extreme on social issues and the economy as they played defense in reliably red states.
 Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida: Senator Ashley Moody defeated Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat, in a tight contest to complete the term of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
 But Democrats were mounting strong challenges all over the map. In Texas, James Talarico, a state lawmaker, is trying to flip a seat in a race against Ken Paxton, the state attorney general. In South Carolina, Senator Darline Graham has been filling the seat long occupied by her late brother, Lindsey, and Democrats have hoped that Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, could flip the seat. In Ohio — which also features an acrimonious race for governor — former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is vying for a comeback as he tries to oust Senator Jon Husted, a Republican.
 The last polling places will not close until 1 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday, in Alaska. Full results won’t be known until well into the evening — and maybe not for days or longer , particularly if many of the races are close — but it’s clear that voters were eager to have their say. Turnout appeared strong across the country , as millions of people cast votes that will deliver a verdict on an unpopular president who has implored the country to act as if he were on the ballot.
 In each of the major Senate battlegrounds, early turnout eclipsed that of the last midterm cycle. In Texas, overall turnout could exceed 10 million votes, which would top the total from each of the last two midterms. In Georgia, Election Day turnout was on track to beat that of the 2024 presidential election, the Georgia secretary of state said.
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more › 
 The counting process: Control of the Senate will hinge on the outcomes in the battleground states of Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Here’s when to expect results › 
 Big spending: This is the most expensive midterm election, as measured in spending on political advertising, since at least 2018, according to data from AdImpact. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, alone contributed $474 million to Republican groups, candidates and their allies, more than any donor has ever spent in a single election cycle. Read more › 
 Minor disruptions: A technical problem with voting machines in Westchester County, N.Y., outside New York City , led officials there to collect ballots by hand in a competitive House race. In Florida, flooding forced more than 20 polling stations across eight counties to be relocated. In North Carolina, technical problems at several precincts caused minor delays; state election officials said they would delay the release of election results to at least 8:15 p.m. from 7:30 p.m. Read more › 
 Election integrity: Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that Mr. Trump’s attacks on the integrity of U.S. elections could lead to tensions during voting and baseless challenges to the outcome. The administration has sought to prove that many noncitizens have cast ballots, but few people have been charged with offenses related to voting fraud. Local and state officials say they are well prepared to run a secure election .
 Court rulings: A federal judge has turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots. And the Supreme Court issued what appeared to be an extraordinary rebuke to Mr. Trump, signaling that it was not interested in assisting his efforts to interfere with how states administer elections.

 Virginia voters have approved a ballot measure repealing language in the state Constitution prohibiting marriage between same-sex couples, The Associated Press reported.
 The ban has been unenforceable since the 2015 Supreme Court ruling that established same-sex marriage as a national right, but would come back into effect if that ruling were overturned. The measure establishes a right to marriage between consenting adults “regardless of sex, gender or race.”

 White House reporter The mood inside President Trump’s watch event in the East Room is fairly lackluster and devoid of energy, according to people on hand. 
 Trump’s history of election night events in that room is not stellar: In 2018, he huddled with Mike Pence’s adviser Nick Ayers, who the president wanted to make his own White House chief of staff, before Ayers turned it down. That night, several high-profile Republican elected officials stayed away from the White House. And 2020 was marked by the president’s infamous declaration that “frankly, we did win” the election, after Arizona was called for President Joseph R. Biden Jr.
 Nov. 3, 2026, 9:26 p.m. ET Rick Rojas 
 Reporting from Atlanta
 Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, wins the governor’s race in Georgia, a breakthrough for Black women. 
 Image Keisha Lance Bottoms during a rally in Morrow, Ga., last month. Credit... Brynn Anderson/Associated Press Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, was elected on Tuesday governor of Georgia , The Associated Press said, as a state shaped by the legacies of slavery, segregation and the fight for civil rights became the first to choose a Black woman as its chief executive.
 Ms. Bottoms, 56, also became the first Democrat elected governor in Georgia in more than 25 years. Her victory against Rick Jackson, the Republican in the race and a billionaire entrepreneur, affirms Georgia’s transformation over the past decade from reliably Republican to a swing state.
 From the start of the race, Ms. Bottoms positioned herself as an unrelenting foil to President Trump in a state that he had won two years ago but where he had considerable baggage. Those include a criminal indictment stemming from his schemes to overturn his defeat in 2020 and a long list of statewide candidates who had his blessing but were rejected by voters. 
 Like Democrats elsewhere, she sought to harness the frustrations of voters who blamed Mr. Trump for inflation, rising fuel prices, challenges accessing affordable health care and an unpopular war with Iran.
 She had also zeroed in on protecting access to the polls and safeguards for minority representation after the Supreme Court’s decision this year that weakened much of what remains of the Voting Rights Act , one of the principal achievements of the civil rights movement that had been grounded in Atlanta. The issue had already been a potent one among many Black voters in Georgia after Republicans responded to the gains made by Democrats in recent elections by adding restrictions on voting access.
 To win, Ms. Bottoms had to overcome doubts in her own party and even in her hometown about her viability in a statewide election. She had been dogged by concerns and resentments from her time leading Atlanta from 2018 to 2022, which ended with her declining to run for re-election, as crime increased and her support eroded.
 In the governors race, she surprised her skeptics by winning the primary outright after breaking ahead of a crowded field of other Democrats who had hoped to force her into a runoff. The win also gave her a head start on wooing swing voters while Republicans were still mired in a very expensive runoff for the nomination.
 Image Rick Jackson, a billionaire entrepreneur, at a campaign rally in Dalton, Ga., last month. Credit... Eric Lee/Getty Images She beat Mr. Jackson, who’d had an unexpected ascent of his own. A political novice with virtually no statewide name recognition, Mr. Jackson entered the race late and pit himself against three candidates who had each twice been elected to statewide office.
 Mr. Jackson laid out a rags-to-riches story, growing up in poverty and neglect and emerging from foster care to become one of Georgia’s wealthiest men. His money came largely from medical staffing companies but also from businesses and investments related to real estate, a Texas data center and faith-based film productions. In all, he poured more than $100 million of his own money into the campaign, far outspending Ms. Bottoms.

 Ned Lamont wins a third term as Connecticut governor, a rare feat. 
 Image Gov. Ned Lamont of Connecticut defeated a Republican challenger half his age to remain in the state’s highest office. Credit... Aaron Flaum/Hartford Courant, via Associated Press Gov. Ned Lamont of Connecticut on Tuesday joined a select few politicians who have been elected to a third term leading the state, according to The Associated Press . He overmatched Ryan Fazio, a Republican state senator, tightening Democrats’ grip on power.
 Mr. Lamont, 72, is only the second Connecticut governor to earn a third consecutive term in the past 200 years. The first was John G. Rowland, a former rising star in the Republican Party who resigned from office in 2004 because of a corruption scandal. He was twice imprisoned and received a pardon from President Trump.
 During World War II, Raymond Baldwin, a Republican, was elected to three nonconsecutive terms of two years each. (Governors in the state now serve four-year terms.)
 On the campaign trail and in television ads, Mr. Lamont sought to tie Mr. Fazio’s candidacy to what the governor argued was the extreme agenda of Republicans, led by Mr. Trump, on immigration, education, cuts to the social safety net, gun control laws and the environment.
 Mr. Lamont, who was first elected in 2018, said that Mr. Fazio’s election would undo the progress he had made toward wiping away fiscal deficits and cutting taxes for middle-income residents.
 Mr. Fazio, 36, who represents Greenwich and parts of Stamford and New Canaan, entered the race with little name recognition and failed to gain significant traction, trailing the governor by double digits in a mid-October Quinnipiac University poll .
 In stark contrast with Mr. Fazio, who was running for statewide office for the first time, Mr. Lamont has spent the better part of two decades getting acquainted with voters in Connecticut.
 His introduction came in 2006 as a little-known primary challenger to Senator Joseph I. Lieberman, a Democrat and former vice-presidential nominee who was heavily favored to win re-election.
 Tapping into Democratic opposition to the U.S. war in Iraq, Mr. Lamont achieved a stunning upset in the primary , only to lose in the general election to Mr. Lieberman, who petitioned his way onto the ballot as an independent and later caucused with Democrats.
 In 2010, Mr. Lamont ran for governor, but lost in the Democratic primary to Dannel P. Malloy, who served two terms.
 Since his successful second run for the state’s highest office, Mr. Lamont, a J.P. Morgan scion from Greenwich who expanded his wealth in the cable television industry, has enjoyed durable approval numbers.
 He has developed a reputation of avoiding flare-ups with political foes on both sides of the aisle and has managed, unlike several of his blue-state counterparts, to avoid the wrath of Mr. Trump.
 Mr. Fazio had sought to present Mr. Lamont as a plutocrat who was detached from everyday concerns about the high costs of living and doing business in Connecticut, pointing to what he argued were crippling taxes and electricity rates.
 The challenger’s path to the ballot was virtually untested.
 In May, two days before Connecticut Republicans were scheduled to choose a nominee, Erin Stewart, one of Mr. Fazio’s chief rivals, withdrew from the race amid fraud accusations tied to her time as mayor of New Britain. She endorsed Mr. Fazio, who easily secured the nomination.
 Casting himself in television ads as Connecticut’s Clark Kent and as a healer saving a patient from death, Mr. Fazio accused Mr. Lamont of undercutting local control over zoning and supporting a tax climate favorable to data centers. (Mr. Lamont supported a 2021 law that provided tax incentive agreements to some data centers, but has since said he opposes the largest such facilities.)
 But that criticism did not land with voters in reliably blue Connecticut, which has not elected a Republican to statewide office in 20 years. The last was M. Jodi Rell, a former lieutenant governor who replaced Mr. Rowland after his resignation and then secured a full term as governor in 2006.

 Reporting from South Carolina Pia Dandiya, a Democrat, wins an open congressional seat in Florida. 
 Image Pia Dandiya won a race centered on the economy and corruption. Credit... Pia Dandiya for Congress Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, won an open congressional seat in Florida on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press , notching a victory for Democrats in a Republican-leaning district seen as a bellwether for both parties.
 Ms. Dandiya defeated Casey Askar, a Republican businessman and former Marine, in Florida’s new 22nd Congressional District, which stretches west from Broward County to Marco Island on the state’s Gulf Coast.
 Republican state lawmakers reshaped the district this year, one of four they gerrymandered to favor their party. President Trump won the district by 10 percentage points in 2024, but the race between Ms. Dandiya, of Palm Beach Gardens, and Mr. Askar, of Naples, proved quite competitive.
 Neither candidate was well known to voters before the election, making their matchup a barometer of how a generic Republican candidate might do against a generic Democratic candidate in a tough year for Republicans. As in much of the country, the race centered on the economy and corruption.
 Florida tends to report election results earlier and faster than many other states. Those results can offer clues about how other races might go. Democrats did well nationally in the last two midterm elections, in 2022 and 2018, yet have struggled in Florida, which has become more Republican leaning.
 Ms. Dandiya, whose parents immigrated from India, is set to become Florida’s first South Asian member of Congress.
 Show more Nov. 3, 2026, 9:12 p.m. ET David Ovalle 
 Byron Donalds, a staunch Trump supporter, wins the Florida governor’s race. 
 Image Byron Donalds at a rally in Clearwater, Fla., last month. Credit... Jacob Langston for The New York Times Representative Byron Donalds, a Republican, won the Florida governor’s race on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press , maintaining his party’s nearly three-decade hold on the seat.
 Mr. Donalds, of Naples, will become Florida’s first Black governor.
 He defeated David Jolly, a former Republican congressman turned Democrat, who gave Mr. Donalds a real race even though Mr. Donalds far out-raised and outspent him. Republicans have held the Florida governor’s office since 1999, and now hold all statewide offices and supermajorities in the Legislature.
 With frequent appearances on Fox News in recent years, Mr. Donalds became known as a staunch supporter of President Trump, who endorsed him to succeed Gov. Ron DeSantis. Mr. Donalds, 48, was first elected to Congress in 2020, and endorsed Mr. Trump over Mr. DeSantis in the 2024 presidential primary.
 Image David Jolly at a campaign event in Coconut Creek, Fla., last month. Credit... Rebecca Blackwell/Associated Press But with voters souring on Mr. Trump, the race against Mr. Jolly became surprisingly competitive, polling showed.
 Mr. Donalds, who was raised in Brooklyn and moved to Florida for college, pitched voters on keeping the state a conservative bastion after Mr. DeSantis leaves office because of term limits. In recent years, Mr. DeSantis pushed divisive measures to counter what he described as “woke” policies in public schools, universities, libraries and local governments. Through it all, he remained popular in the state.
 Mr. Donalds has vowed to make Florida more affordable by lowering property taxes and insurance costs, streamlining government agencies and spurring business innovation. He has also championed using taxpayer funds to expand school choice alongside his wife, Erika Donalds, who runs a private education company.
 Mr. Donalds raised more than $170 million, more than six times as much as Mr. Jolly did. During the campaign, critics portrayed Mr. Donalds as beholden to big-money interest groups and companies that build or support data centers, which voters in both parties largely oppose.

 Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is re-elected to the House for the fifth time. 
 Image Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won her race to keep her seat in the House in a district comprising parts of Queens and the Bronx. Credit... Eric Lee for The New York Times Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the 37-year-old democratic socialist from Queens, defeated her Republican opponent, Diamant Hysenaj, on Tuesday, winning a fifth term in Congress, according to The Associated Press .
 Mr. Hysenaj, 44, a real estate developer, never mounted much of a challenge to the congresswoman, raising only $440,000 this election cycle, an amount dwarfed by Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s $38 million haul.
 So confident was she in her popularity in New York’s 14th Congressional District, encompassing portions of the Bronx and Queens — including segments of the so-called Commie Corridor that helped elect Mayor Zohran Mamdani — that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez spent much of the election season barnstorming elsewhere.
 She traveled across New York State campaigning for other Democrats, including Gov. Kathy Hochul, and she crisscrossed the country campaigning for national contenders, too, including Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a Senate candidate in Michigan, and Angie Nixon , a Senate candidate in Florida.
 Her backing was more than rhetorical. She donated $300,000 to New York State Democrats and transferred $1 million to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund.
 Her campaign-season support for other Democrats comes as Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is openly considering a run for president or for the Senate, a decision she has said she will make after the midterms.
 “There’s an argument that some make that this is a very unique political window and, oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot,” she said recently, adding, “life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

Dave Sanders for The New York Times Gov. Kathy Hochul , a Democrat whose folksy, centrist approach has helped her forge relationships with leaders as disparate as President Trump and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, won a second full term as governor of New York on Tuesday, according to The Associated Press .
 Ms. Hochul, the state’s first female governor, defeated Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive, a Republican who is a longtime friend of Mr. Trump’s. Their alliance proved auspicious for Ms. Hochul, a Buffalo native who spent months bashing her opponent for supporting the Trump administration’s policies.
 But Ms. Hochul, 68, has also displayed an ability to work with the president, despite their profound differences. She worked with the Trump administration on new energy projects, including the jump-starting of several stalled natural gas pipeline projects , and has looked for moments to influence the administration’s immigration enforcement in the state .
 At the same time, the governor fought the Trump administration’s efforts to kill the congestion pricing program, which is on track to raise $15 billion for transit improvements by charging vehicles to enter the Manhattan business district.
 At one point, Mr. Trump posted on social media , “CONGESTION PRICING IS DEAD. Manhattan, and all of New York, is SAVED. LONG LIVE THE KING!” In response Ms. Hochul said : “We are a nation of laws, not ruled by a king. We’ll see you in court.” (New York ended up prevailing in court, and the toll remained in effect).
 The Associated Press called the race just as the polls closed at 9 p.m., prompting rounds of cheers in the ballroom at the New York Hilton Midtown, where Ms. Hochul was holding an election night party with top state Democratic officials.
 Ms. Hochul’s re-election bid became as much a referendum on the actions coming from the White House as on policies flowing from the State Capitol in Albany, N.Y. The governor’s campaign focused on Mr. Blakeman’s fidelity to Mr. Trump in its tens of millions of dollars in attack ads against her rival.
 “We have a real record of accomplishment,” she said on Sunday at a Queens sports bar while campaigning with Mr. Mamdani and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
 “When you’re delivering universal child care, when you’re delivering record investments in education, when you’re delivering health care despite all the Trump administration cutbacks, when you’re focusing on affordability and what we can do to help lift up New Yorkers,” Ms. Hochul said, “that is the message that is resonating.”
 Despite his best efforts, Mr. Blakeman, 71, a longtime player in Republican politics on Long Island, struggled to shake loose from his association with Mr. Trump.
 After winning re-election as county executive last fall, Mr. Blakeman entered the governor’s race, setting up a primary against Representative Elise Stefanik, a well-known staunch defender of Mr. Trump. But Ms. Stefanik abruptly dropped out and announced that she would not seek re-election to the House.
 Mr. Blakeman used his campaign messaging to try to attract disaffected Democrats and independent voters who have been burdened by rising energy costs and high taxes.
 But he was dogged by fund-raising challenges and temporarily waylaid by irregularities in his required filings to the state. At one point he was removed from the campaign finance matching program and had to sue to regain access.
 In the end he spent around $24 million on ads, according to AdImpact, just a bit shy of what Ms. Hochul spent, and benefited from help from a group that was seeded with donations from James Dolan , the owner of the New York Knicks.
 For Ms. Hochul, winning a second term strengthens her own legacy, and opens the door for her to match two recent predecessors, Mario M. Cuomo and George E. Pataki, who each served three full terms.
 She entered office in August 2021, moving up from lieutenant governor after Andrew M. Cuomo resigned amid sexual harassment allegations that he denies. Her first year in office was defined by efforts to stabilize state government, which was still dealing with the pandemic and the fallout of scandals related to Mr. Cuomo.
 Her election to a full term in 2022 proved to be closer than expected, leading Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker, to accuse Ms. Hochul of dragging down the Democratic ticket when the party lost five House seats in the state. She struggled initially to pass big-ticket policy items related to housing and to win approval for her preferred pick for the state’s top judge.
 She also drew criticism for initially withdrawing her support of congestion pricing, only to reverse her decision shortly after her election, while lowering the charge from $15 to $9 for most vehicles.
 Throughout much of her first full term, Ms. Hochul, a former Erie County clerk, was viewed warily by legions of progressive voters in New York City. She began to find her footing after Mr. Trump’s re-election in 2024, when she became a vocal bulwark against Washington.
 Still, faced with middling approval numbers and numerous rivals from both parties preparing to challenge her, she seemed far from certain to win a year ago. But several primary challenges from Democrats either sputtered or never materialized.
 One such bid came from her lieutenant governor, Antonio Delgado, who had hoped to challenge her from the left. His campaign was undermined by Ms. Hochul’s relationship with Mr. Mamdani, who endorsed the governor last winter. Mr. Delgado dropped out after the state party convention and was replaced on the ticket with Adrienne Adams, the former speaker of the New York City Council.
 Mr. Mamdani’s support followed a similar gesture from Ms. Hochul, who became one of the most prominent Democrats to endorse him during his mayoral run. Since his victory, the two have built a surprisingly fruitful governing partnership despite profound ideological differences on a number of fronts, including raising taxes and support for Israel.
 Ultimately, Mr. Mamdani’s support for Ms. Hochul appeared to be crucial, helping her to excite the younger, more progressive coalition of voters that propelled his mayoral campaign to victory last year. Over the last month they appeared together repeatedly; Mr. Mamdani also filmed several videos highlighting their work together to expand child care and resolve the city’s budgetary woes.

 Trump officials pledge to arrest noncitizen voters. 
 Image People vote at a polling station in Manhattan on Tuesday. Credit... Hiroko Masuike/The New York Times As polls closed in several states on Tuesday evening, there were no signs that federal immigration agents had been deployed in large numbers to voting sites, a widespread concern among civil rights groups and immigrant advocates leading up to the election.
 But Trump administration officials made clear in a flurry of social media posts on Tuesday that noncitizens who illegally voted would be hunted down. Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, also indicated that federal agents would scour voter records after the midterm elections to try to find unlawful voters.
 “If you vote illegally, we will find you,” Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in one post. “We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape.”
 ICE’s account also promoted about a half dozen arrests throughout the day, posting photos depicting handcuffed immigrants accused of illegally voting, mostly in past elections. “ANOTHER VOTER FRAUD ARREST!” the agency wrote in one post .
 The remarks signaled that the administration planned to continue its search for noncitizens who illegally registered to vote or actually voted, an effort that it has already dedicated massive resources to. Many studies have found noncitizen voting to be rare, but President Trump has falsely called the issue rampant. Mr. Mullin and other administration officials have said that any amount of noncitizen voting is unacceptable.
 In a Fox News interview on Tuesday, Mr. Mullin said he had “made it very clear that ICE agents aren’t going to be around polling places unless there’s a threat.” But he indicated that his department would scrutinize voter data after the election.
 “After this election we’ll be gathering all the data. We’ll be gathering the voting logs, and we’ll be going through those and making sure that no illegals voted,” Mr. Mullin said.
 The number of people who have been charged so far make up a small share of the more than 158 million ballots cast in the 2024 general election. The administration has charged about 240 people with voting fraud-related offenses since Mr. Trump returned to office, according to the Justice Department.
 As of Oct. 15, 25 people had been found guilty or pleaded guilty , a New York Times review of court records found. Two had been acquitted, and charges were dropped or cases were dismissed in four other instances.
 Several election experts and immigrant advocacy groups have denounced the efforts, saying that the administration’s intense focus on the issue was not producing evidence that noncitizen voting was widespread, and that it instead could be intimidating voters.

 The Senate will get its first openly gay male senator. 
 Image Representative Chris Pappas visited a polling place on Primary Day in Concord, N.H., in September. Credit... John Tully for The New York Times Representative Chris Pappas, Democrat of New Hampshire, will be the Senate’s first openly gay male senator with his victory over former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican, on Tuesday.
 Like other candidates on the precipice of breaking a barrier, he did not spend much time emphasizing the milestone on the campaign trail. But it is a notable breakthrough in the Senate, as L.G.B.T.Q. rights have faced pushback in some states and some gay rights activists have warned about a decline in public support.
 While his husband was in attendance at some of his campaign events, Mr. Pappas largely focused his message on the themes that most Democrats highlighted: a pledge to deal with high prices and health care costs, and opposition to Washington corruption, among others.
 “I think people, regardless of their politics, really just want their neighbors to be able to be themselves,” Mr. Pappas told The New York Times in October.
 Representative Barney Frank, Democrat of Massachusetts, voluntarily came out as gay in 1987, after six years of service in the House. Decades later, Tammy Baldwin, Democrat of Wisconsin, in 2012 became the first openly gay person elected to the Senate.
 Before his career in politics took off, Mr. Pappas, 46, was probably most associated with his family’s restaurant in Manchester, N.H., the Puritan Backroom. His grandfather is said to have invented the chicken tender there.
 At 22, Mr. Pappas ran for state representative in New Hampshire, winning the race. That set off a winding political career in the state, before he joined the wave of Democrats in 2018 that capitalized on anger against President Trump during his first term.
 Mr. Pappas has served for four terms in the House and is a chair of the Congressional Equality Caucus. He will replace Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who did not seek re-election after three terms.
 Jess Bidgood contributed reporting.
